subject: Why pink boots are causing problems for World Cup commentators
body:
When Vicki Sparks takes her seat in the broadcast booth for a World Cup game, she takes out her print-out of the two matchday rosters and scours the field during the warm-ups.

As a commentator for the UK’s BBC Sport, one of her first steps in the stadium is to look out for any clues which may help differentiate between the stars in the match ahead. She will scribble little notes by each player’s name.

Play-by-play announcers are often positioned towards the very top of vast stadiums, reducing the players to ant-like specks far below. Of course, they have already done hours of preparation, but no stone is left unturned as they seek every marginal gain from the gantry, eager to ensure that the game’s definitive moments can be called with confidence.

subject: Vibes will dictate Burnham’s election timetable
body: Plus: why socialists should embrace luxury apartments ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ All newsletters | Read this in your browser VIBES WILL DICTATE BURNHAM’S TRUE ELECTION TIMETABLE Tony Tassell Financial Opinion Editor ‌ ‌ July 17 2026 One of the few messages of absolute clarity from Andy Burnham is that there will not be an early election after he becomes prime minister, writes Robert Shrimsley in his latest column. He says given the state of the opinion polls, this cannot have been a hard call. Even so, what classifies as early? Robert points out that we can be fairly sure Burnham will not call an election in the next 12 months but there are good reasons for him to want to head to the polls well before he must in July 2029. “And while he may not be thinking about it now, circumstances change. This is one decision leaders keep very tight,” he writes. Robert says an early clue to Burnham’s instincts will be how much pain he crams into his first Budget. “The more he front-loads the discomfort the longer he gives himself,” he says, adding there is one potential sweet spot for an election date. Elsewhere, Tej Parikh argues socialists should embrace luxury apartments. He says high-end developments can be more effective at unlocking affordability than social housing programmes. Gillian Tett warns on the dangers of investor fatalism. Reports of a Russo-Chinese plan to disable satellites underline how markets are ignoring geopolitical threats to the tech boom. And Mohamed El-Erian writes on the lessons Burnham must heed on the economy. One is the need to tackle the bureaucratic set-up that has been a key reason for poor implementation of policy in recent years. “This includes a Treasury that seems inclined to repeatedly fall into the trap of reducing complex, multidimensional economic strategy to mere budget arithmetic,” he says. WHAT YOU’VE BEEN SAYING ‌ ‌ Letter: When investing starts to look like gambling Letter from Anna Pavlova, Professor of Finance, London Business School The issue is not whether innovation should be encouraged, but whether participants understand the risks and incentives behind increasingly engaging, game-like financial products. The appeal of prediction markets is often driven as much by competition and instant feedback as by investment fundamentals. Financial innovation can improve markets, but trust depends on ensuring that greater access is matched by greater understanding. subject: Burnham plans policy blitz
body: Plus, BoE bond sales and Accor’s chief executive ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ All newsletters | Read this in your browser Irwin Cruz Digital Editor ‌ ‌ July 17 2026 Good morning, happy Friday and welcome to FirstFT. In today’s newsletter: * Andy Burnham plans blitz of policy announcements * Investors say BoE should slow or stop long-dated bond sales * Accor hired law firm to investigate conduct of CEO Sébastien Bazin * Meet the billionaire scions fighting to escape the family shadow ‌ We begin with Andy Burnham, whose formal accession to power starts today. Leadership change: The MP for Makerfield will begin his transition to head of the government today when he is officially announced as the new leader of the Labour Party at a special conference in London. The handover as prime minister will take place on Monday when Sir Keir Starmer tenders his resignation to King Charles. Burnham will then travel to Buckingham Palace to formally assume office. Policy blitz: Burnham will next week seek to hit the ground running as UK prime minister with early announcements on the cost of living, North Sea energy, social care and devolution, according to people briefed on his plans. Burnham will enter Number 10 next Monday lunchtime and start forming his cabinet. Allies say his Downing Street speech to the nation will set out his core objectives. Meanwhile, Whitehall insiders say a “nascent grid” of early announcements is taking shape. Burnham’s allies also note he will go on regional visits to highlight his commitment to shifting power outside London. Read the full story. * Project ‘ABC’: Burnham will today be anointed Labour leader at the third time of asking after what a key ally has claimed was a year of planning. * Opinion: The incoming government’s economic policy must go beyond mere announcements and budget arithmetic, writes Mohamed El-Erian, professor of practice at Wharton School. Here’s what else I’m keeping tabs on today and over the weekend: * Economic data: The EU releases June inflation data. * World Cup final: Reigning champions Argentina face Spain in New Jersey on Sunday. FIVE MORE TOP STORIES 1. Big bond investors expect the Bank of England to slow or even stop its sales of long-term UK government debt this autumn, amid concerns that its so-called quantitative tightening is piling pressure on a fragile gilt market. 2. Exclusive: The board of hotel group Accor hired an elite Paris law firm to carry out a probe into the conduct of chief executive Sébastien Bazin, in response to allegations of conflicts of interest and favouritism under his leadership. Read the full story. 3. Exclusive: French conglomerate Dassault Systèmes is in talks to buy drug trial software maker ArisGlobal from Nordic Capital for about $2bn, in what would represent the latest successful exit for the Swedish private equity group. The potential deal would extend Dassault’s push into software used in life sciences. 4. Exclusive: Anglian Water has handed its chief executive £1.3mn in retention and other payments in a move that appears to sidestep the regulator’s powers to clamp down on bonuses. Read the full story. 5. US President Donald Trump used a lengthy primetime speech last night to cast doubt on the integrity of US elections, claiming “shocking vulnerabilities” in the electoral system and accusing China of a widespread effort to hurt his campaign in the 2020 election that he lost to Joe Biden. HEIRS APPARENT From left: Miltiadis Marinakis, Thlopie Motsepe, Mario Ho, Halima Dangote and Parth Jindal © FT montage/Getty Images/Reuters/PA Many millennial and Gen-Z members of the world’s biggest family businesses are preparing to take up the hereditary mantle. With more than $60tn poised to pass into their hands in the US alone before 2048 as part of the “great wealth transfer”, the role they play in family firms, philanthropy and their own enterprises will be of vital economic importance. Some heirs are preparing to take over family businesses, but others are using their financial freedom to turn passions into businesses or start their own companies. Here are the billionaire scions fighting to escape their families’ shadow. WE’RE ALSO READING . . . * Investor fatalism: Reports of a plan by Russia and China to disable satellites underline how markets are ignoring geopolitical threats to the tech boom, writes Gillian Tett. * Iran’s return to war: Tehran believes that further escalation will force the US to offer the security and economic relief the country craves, writes Vali Nasr, professor at Johns Hopkins University. * Dependency risk: An investor that backed Spotify and Revolut has warned that Europe’s reliance on US technology has become a strategic vulnerability. CHART OF THE DAY Are we really entering an AI-induced jobs apocalypse? Companies in sectors ranging from consulting to engineering are updating their hiring practices and training programmes, rather than cutting graduate positions. The heaviest adopters of the technology are actually bringing in more entry-level employees, whose roles are being reshaped for the AI era. TAKE A BREAK FROM THE NEWS . . . From Lionel Messi to Erling Haaland, individual stars have shone brighter than ever at this World Cup. subject: It feels really good to build with your hands
body: Hi Umair! How’s it going?? 😊 I've been doing something lately that I haven't done in a long time. Building with my hands. Actual physical hardware. Components. Devices you can hold. And I forgot how good it feels. I've spent years in front of screens. Writing, recording, coding, editing. All digital. You ship something, and it just exists somewhere on the internet. But there's something completely different about making a physical thing. You can hold it. You can show someone, and they can touch it. It exists in the real world in a way that a YouTube video or a piece of software just doesn't. I'm still very early with all of this; I'm not going to pretend I know what I'm doing yet. But what's surprised me is how accessible it's become. Hardware always felt like a completely separate world to me. Like it required a different kind of brain, or years of training I didn't have. But with AI helping me learn faster and debug the code that runs these devices, the gap between "person who builds software" and "person who builds hardware" has shrunk enormously. I started tinkering. And for the first time in a long time, I felt like a beginner in the best possible way. That feeling of not knowing what you're doing but being genuinely excited to figure it out? I think that's one of the best feelings there is. More to come on what I'm actually building soon. subject: Zelenskyy’s political crisis
body: Plus, China’s largest AI model to date and South Korea’s first rate rise in three years ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ All newsletters | Read this in your browser Benjamin Wilhelm Newsletter Editor ‌ ‌ July 17 2026 Good morning, happy Friday and welcome to FirstFT. In today’s newsletter: * Ukraine plunged into political turmoil * Takanomics vs Abenomics: the $2.3tn prizefight * The perks of parenting by spreadsheet ‌ We begin in Ukraine, where President Volodymyr Zelenskyy is facing a political crisis after firing his defence minister. What to know: Zelenskyy was on Thursday facing one of the biggest displays of dissent since Russia’s 2022 full-scale invasion after his move to oust Mykhailo Fedorov prompted a public and political backlash. The firing late on Wednesday of the 35-year-old defence minister after only six months prompted angry demonstrations across Ukraine and the resignation of a senior air force commander. Zelenskyy spent much of the day in talks with his chief of staff, former head of military intelligence Kyrylo Budanov, seeking to co-ordinate a path out of the turmoil, aides to the president said. After lawmakers suggested Zelenskyy’s party could not garner enough votes for his preferred replacement — Ihor Klymenko, previously interior minister — the president was forced into a concession, instead putting forward the acting head of Ukraine’s SBU security service, Yevhenii Khmara. Fedorov said in a press conference on Thursday that he had rejected an offer to stay on as a presidential adviser and framed his firing as the fruit of a power struggle with Ukraine’s top general, Oleksandr Syrskyi, over his efforts to modernise the defence department. Why the defence minister was popular: Fedorov was appointed only in January, but he is credited with accelerating procurement and drone production by the notoriously opaque ministry. Ukraine’s innovative use of mass-produced drones is seen as having helped slow Russia’s advances in recent months. Defence industry officials, senior Ukrainian officials, MPs from Zelenskyy’s party and others familiar with the matter have also said — some publicly — that Fedorov had been a barrier to interests seeking to profit from Ukraine’s vast wartime defence budget. Read more about the political turmoil in Ukraine. * FT View: Zelenskyy’s sacking of the defence minister is a setback for the country’s military efforts, writes the Editorial Board. Here’s what else I’m keeping tabs on today and over the weekend: * Economic data: Malaysia reports June inflation data and advance second-quarter GDP. Hong Kong publishes June jobs figures and Singapore releases non-oil domestic export data. * World Cup final: Reigning champions Argentina face Spain in East Rutherford, New Jersey on Sunday. WAS THIS FORWARDED TO YOU? If you’re an FT subscriber, sign up here to get this newsletter delivered straight to your inbox. If you’re new to the FT, take out a subscription here. Sent every weekday. FIVE MORE TOP STORIES 1. Chinese AI start-up Moonshot is set to release a large language model with capabilities approaching those of frontier US labs such as Anthropic, as the gap narrows between the two countries on state of the art AI. Read more about Kimi K3, China’s largest AI model to date. * More tech news: Chipmaker TSMC said it plans to invest another $100bn to expand production in the US. * US-China tech war: The US House China committee chair has urged the Trump administration to ban US companies from buying memory chips from China’s CXMT and YMTC. 2. South Korea’s central bank raised its benchmark interest rate by 0.25 percentage points to 2.75 per cent, kicking off a monetary tightening cycle aimed at containing inflationary pressures spurred by the AI-driven semiconductor boom. Yesterday’s move was the Bank of Korea’s first rate increase in more than three years. 3. Donald Trump’s longtime teleprompter operator is under investigation by US regulators for placing prediction market bets on the president’s statements in public speeches, people familiar with the matter have said. Gabriel Perez allegedly used insider knowledge of the president’s speeches to profit on “mention markets” on Kalshi. * More US news: The Trump family’s media group is asking large trading firms to pay for ultrafast access to the US president’s often market-moving posts on Truth Social. 4. Netflix’s shares fell more than 8 per cent on Thursday despite as-expected earnings after the streaming giant forecast its worst revenue growth in three years. Its projection of 11.7 per cent year-on-year growth in the third quarter came in below Wall Street consensus and would mark the slowest expansion since 2023. 5. Panamanian officials are heading to Beijing in an effort to end a dispute that has seen hundreds of vessels leave its shipping registry after a major step-up in detentions by Chinese authorities. The clash escalated in February when the Central American country, under heavy US pressure, took control of two ports run by Hong Kong-based CK Hutchison. HUNGARY’S NEW ERA © Filip Singer/EPA Since Péter Magyar and his Tisza party swept into power after defeating the illiberal nationalist prime minister Viktor Orbán, Magyar has taken sweeping moves to dismantle his predecessor’s machinery. This week his government amended the constitution to remove the president, Tamás Sulyok, an Orbán ally. It is also strengthening anti-corruption bodies, reinforcing judicial independence, dismantling agencies and foundations controlled by the Fidesz party and removing Orbán-era appointees from state energy companies, banks and regulators. But the scale of the change is such that even staunch opponents of Orbán’s authoritarianism question whether Magyar was moving too far too fast, while others detect a populist streak and fret about his ability to take unpopular decisions. Is Hungary witnessing a revolution under Magyar or is it just exchanging one strongman for another? WE’RE ALSO READING . . . * Takanomics vs Abenomics: Japan’s new prime minister has broken with her mentor by encouraging firms to invest according to a government plan, writes Leo Lewis. * Indian business: Foreign acquisitions by Indian companies are on track to hit a record this year, putting further pressure on a weak rupee. * California wealth tax: An effort to tackle inequality in America’s most progressive state is pitting populist anger against super-rich power. CHART OF THE DAY Since her first child was born, Soumaya Keynes had been filling in a parenting spreadsheet to monitor how close she and her husband were to a shared objective: dividing childcare as evenly as possible. The psychology behind this 👇🏻 Remember, you want a second account for this because this makes it look like that you are speaking from a third party recommending a tool or a service. So what you do is you comment under the post of the person with a problem, and then you link the original post on the first account that has the links to your service or product. So people see your comment, they'll click that link to the original post. You see the original post and they click the links to your business. If you comment early enough under a Reddit post that gets a lot of views, you'll be getting a ton of inbound leads to your business's website. And as long as your funnel is set up, you should be getting booked calls. Follow me for transparent advice as I scale my business to $10M ARR. subject: Lionel Messi sets up stunning World Cup comeback to put Argentina in final, did Tuchel cause England collapse?
body:
Lionel Messi and Argentina will play Spain in the World Cup final on Sunday after they scored twice in six minutes and 24 seconds at the end of a ferocious semi-final to break English hearts.

England had led from the 55th minute through Anthony Gordon and looked set for a first World Cup final since 1966, but as they dropped deeper and deeper, Enzo Fernandez curled in a stunning equaliser from outside the box on 85 minutes and then substitute Lautaro Martinez headed home in the second minute of stoppage time, with Messi assisting both goals. He now has 12 World Cup finals assists, a new record.

It was a game that began in fury and ended in chaos, with Argentina now having scored 11 times from the 75th minute onwards at this tournament.

subject: Invitation to connect with Apple
body: Hi Umair, We’d like to invite you to talk with a hiring team member about career opportunities at Apple. The primary email address on your profile should match the email address on this invitation. If you don’t have a job profile, this is your opportunity to create one. 2. Learn about Apple Retail. subject: Planning for your retirement and other financial goals
body: Dear Mr Umair Aamir A Aziz, I'm Yu Xiang ONG, your DBS Wealth Planning Manager. My role is to help you navigate your financial journey. This includes assessing your current financial plans, providing tailored investment advice, and empowering you with the knowledge to make informed decisions for a secure financial future. A key service I provide is ensuring your financial journey stays on track and your plans remain aligned with your evolving goals and life priorities. With changes such as the recent adjustment to Singapore's retirement age, which is increasing to 64 on July 1, 2026, many Singaporeans are reconsidering their long-term financial strategies. These shifts often bring new considerations, from diversification to managing downside risk. I'm here to help you navigate these changes and assess your current financial plans, taking into account your individual goals, time horizon, and comfort with market fluctuations. If you'd like to arrange a review, simply reply to this email, or you can schedule a call with me at your convenience via digiWealth. Did You Know? Our Chief Investment Office has just launched their Q3 economy outlook. If you are interested, we at DBS made sure that this is available in digiWealth on your digibank app, or the DBS website. Yours sincerely, Yu Xiang ONG Wealth Planning Manager Consumer Banking Group DBS Bank Ltd DBS has introduced additional measures to better protect you against scams, such as the removal of clickable links from emails or SMS sent to customers. However, in managing your account relationship, we may send client communications which contain clickable link(s) at your request and/or when you expect it from us. Such information will be for the sole purpose of providing information to you. If in doubt, please contact me before accessing the links. CONFIDENTIALITY NOTE: This message and any attachments transmitted with it contain confidential information and are intended only for the person to whom it is addressed. subject: Conflicts of interest are back
body: Plus: Takanomics vs Abenomics, the $2.3tn prizefight ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ All newsletters | Read this in your browser CONFLICTS OF INTEREST ARE BACK Srinidhi Balakrishnan Commissioning Editor, FT Opinion ‌ ‌ July 16 2026 The problem with Jared Kushner and Ivanka Trump’s proposal to build a resort on Albania’s coast is greater than just flamingos and ambient sleaze, writes Alec Russell. The signal their plan sends is dire. There is a sense that if you are close to Donald Trump, the normal rules do not apply. What has happened to the old principle of government that required you to park business interests — and fill out disclosure forms? As the list of the Trump circle’s business entanglements grows, it seems ever more likely it will contain the seeds of the Trump project’s decline. Come November, the Democrats should focus their fire on the use of public office by Trump’s circle for private gain. Elsewhere, Leo Lewis shines a light on Japan’s latest ideological prizefight. Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi has broken with her mentor Shinzo Abe and is pursuing an economic strategy of her own. While Takanomics bears some similarities to Abenomics, Japan and the world need to recognise — as a matter of urgency — that they are fundamentally different. John Thornhill argues the New Whittle Laboratory in Cambridge offers Britain a clear, achievable blueprint for innovation. The incoming government of Andy Burnham would do well to recognise this and throw its weight behind enterprise as an engine of national growth. And Jill Rutter, a senior fellow at the Institute for Government, argues the UK is forgetting the dull bit of climate change policy. Adaptation has never been the priority, but this summer’s heat is a message that the Treasury needs to act. WHAT YOU’VE BEEN SAYING ‌ ‌ Military support for Ukraine needs a diplomatic endgame — Letter from A Myilsami, Postgraduate Teacher (Retired), Tamil Nadu, India in response to a report President Volodymyr Zelenskyy’s framing of the war as a contest decided by drones and air defence, rather than territory alone, deserves serious attention from American readers, not just policymakers in Washington. The technology angle is real. A conflict once measured in miles of front line is now measured in interceptor stock and drone production rates. That should worry anyone hoping for a quick resolution, because technological races rarely end wars faster. subject: UK business struggles to contact Burnham
body: Plus, Trump’s BBC lawsuit and energy IPOs ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ All newsletters | Read this in your browser Irwin Cruz Digital Editor ‌ ‌ July 16 2026 Good morning and welcome to FirstFT. In today’s newsletter: * UK business worries about how to reach Burnham * US government looks at joining Trump’s BBC lawsuit * Energy IPOs surge as investors hunt for ways to play AI boom * Under Magyar, is Hungary’s new era at hand? You can listen to today’s top news stories in the FT News Briefing podcast. ‌ We begin in the UK, where industry executives are having a difficult time getting a direct line to prime minister-in-waiting Andy Burnham. What to know: Major UK businesses say that they have been struggling to make contact with Burnham’s team, causing anxiety that the next prime minister will not listen to their concerns. Just days before Burnham enters Downing Street, chief executives and advisers complain they are stuck in one-way traffic when it comes to engaging with the incoming administration because there is no dedicated person to lobby on policy. Why it matters: Executives worry that Burnham’s small team of advisers view business as a low priority while they focus on how to overhaul government structures and spearhead a devolution drive that includes staffing a new “Number 10 North” office in Manchester. The lack of contact is leading to nervousness in the City, especially as most of Burnham’s top ministerial team remains unfilled. “Who do we call to discuss policies? We don’t know and aren’t being told,” said a government affairs adviser to several FTSE companies. Shabana Mahmood: The City, however, has expressed relief at the prospects of the home secretary becoming Burnham’s chancellor. “Shabana is certainly the lesser of evils,” said Sir Martin Sorrell, executive chair of S4 Capital. “She is a serious person and definitely better news than Ed Miliband. The problem remains that Burnham and his team haven’t had long to prepare. She has no time to plan and no financial wriggle room.” * Post analysis: Outgoing Prime Minister Sir Keir Starmer says the UK is “in better shape” than two years ago. What does his record actually say? Here’s what else I’m keeping tabs on today: * Economic data: Italy releases inflation data for June. The UK publishes GDP estimate for May. * Ukraine: President Volodymyr Zelenskyy is expected to unveil his new government, the third cabinet overhaul since the start of Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022. * Results: ABB, Johnson & Johnson, Netflix, United Airlines and US Bancorp report earnings. FIVE MORE TOP STORIES 1. The US government is looking to participate in Donald Trump’s lawsuit against the BBC, in a move that would complicate the defamation dispute. The president is suing the British broadcaster over a documentary that spliced together parts of his speech to supporters on January 6 2021. He is seeking $10bn in damages. 2. Energy companies are raising money at initial public offerings at their fastest pace this century, taking advantage of investors’ hunt for new ways to bet on the boom in power-intensive AI data centres. IPOs for energy groups raised $12.6bn in the first half of this year, according to data firm Dealogic. 3. Greece is opposing a new round of EU sanctions against Russian gas to protect Dynagas, the shipping company belonging to Greek tycoon George Prokopiou that has specialised in transporting Russian cargoes from a liquefied natural gas plant in the Arctic region. 4. Goldman Sachs has taken junior roles on a trio of high-profile British deals after missing out on top billing in recent weeks, an unusual move for the Wall Street investment bank which has been a perennial leader in UK mergers and acquisitions. 5. Argentina have reached the men’s football World Cup final, setting up a face-off with Spain on Sunday, after Lionel Messi inspired a late comeback to extend England’s long wait for a major trophy. Simon Kuper writes why the Three Lions deserved the loss. THE BIG READ © Filip Singer/EPA Since Péter Magyar and his Tisza party swept into power after defeating the illiberal nationalist prime minister Viktor Orbán, Magyar has taken sweeping moves to dismantle his predecessor’s machinery. This week his government amended the constitution to remove the president, Tamás Sulyok, an Orbán ally. It is also strengthening anti-corruption bodies, reinforcing judicial independence, dismantling agencies and foundations controlled by the Fidesz party and removing Orbán-era appointees from state energy companies, banks and regulators. But the scale of the change is such that even staunch opponents of Orbán’s authoritarianism question whether Magyar was moving too far too fast, while others detect a populist streak and fret about his ability to take unpopular decisions. Is Hungary witnessing a revolution under Magyar or is it just exchanging one strongman for another? WE’RE ALSO READING . . . * Conflict of interest returns: Will a brazen culture become an accepted standard, normalising the use of public office for private gain, asks Alec Russell. * UBS in the US: The Swiss bank wants to be valued as a global player but can it match Wall Street rivals in the world’s richest wealth market? * California’s wealth tax: An effort to tackle inequality in America’s most progressive state is pitting populist anger against power of the super-rich. CHART OF THE DAY Since her first child was born, Soumaya Keynes had been filling in a parenting spreadsheet to monitor how close she and her husband were to a shared objective: dividing childcare as evenly as possible. TAKE A BREAK FROM THE NEWS . . . Christopher Nolan’s $250mn retelling of The Odyssey is both crazy and conventional, writes film critic Danny Leigh. Read the review.
